codices.title: Observationes — the observation archive of Tycho Brahe, and the printed catalogue of stars
codices.description: The manuscript volumes in which Tycho Brahe's observations survive — the archetypes and transcripts at the Royal Danish Library, the nineteen annual fair copies and the working star catalogue at the Austrian National Library, and the lost octavo — with Dreyer's description of each, the hand, what it was copied from, the pages of the Opera Omnia set from it, and the events of its custody 1601–1929.

volumes.label: Lost 8vo observation volume 1563–74
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: The small octavo of the earliest observations, 1563–1574, from which Codex A was copied; Dreyer notes from Codex A's marginal notes that it was not entirely in the young Tycho's hand but later augmented.
volumes.notes: The small octavo of the earliest observations, 1563–1574, from which Codex A (GKS 1824) was copied. On Bartholin's receipt of 20 June 1664; seen by Rostgaard in La Hire's room in Paris on 4 May 1697 and returned with the archetypes in 1707; lent from the Royal Library to Christian Hvass about 1778 and never returned; reported in the hands of a Dane living in France in 1804 (Dreyer, TBOO X pp. VIII, X). Its two copies are Codex A and Bartholin's GKS 310.

volumes.label: Observations December 1577 – 1581 (portrait & arms binding)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: The archetype of the years December 1577 – 1581 (the KB catalogue: maxima ex parte autographum); bound in the portrait-and-arms cover after it was written, and Codex A copied from it.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 206 leaves including two endpapers, 19 blank; four loose leaves inserted
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes Astronomicæ a Solstitio Hiberno anni 1577 ad 1581, maxima ex parte Autogr.
volumes.notes: Codex B (Opera Omnia X); Hven 1577–1582. Tycho's portrait and arms on the binding.

volumes.label: Observations 1582–1586
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: The archetype of 1582–1586 (the KB catalogue: ex parte autographum); leaves were lost after Codex V had been transcribed from it.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 494 leaves in folio + 10 leaves in quarto (Elias Olai's German observations of 1584)
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Volumen [I] observationes annorum 1582 usque ad 86 inclus., ex parte autographum.
volumes.notes: Codex C (Opera Omnia X); Hven 1582–1586. Partly autograph; the autograph source recopied into the Vienna fair-copies of 1582–1586 (Cod. 10657–10661). some ten inserted 4° leaves of Elias Olai's German observations at the end of 1584.

volumes.label: Observations 1587–1589 + fixed stars 1590–1594
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: In the first part of this codex (1587–89) Tycho's own hand appears frequently, whereas in the fixed-star observations it is hardly found in even a single place.
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Volumen [II] observationum pro annis 1587-1590 incl., ex parte autogr.
volumes.notes: Codex D (Opera Omnia X); Hven. Sun/Moon/planets for 1587–1589 (1587–88 fixed stars absent; 1589 planetary runs only to 2 June) plus the fixed-star observations for 1590–1594 (the matching planetary records for those years are in Codex E / GKS 313). The V scribe copied these fixed stars in Codex D's order — the source of the 1589–91 fixed-star muddle in the Historia Coelestis.

volumes.label: Observations 1590–1594 (Sun, Moon, planets)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Tycho's hand appears in a number of places (especially for annotations) in this codex as well.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 367 numbered leaves + 5 unnumbered (the KB catalogue agrees: ff. 1–183 + 184–367 + 5)

leaves_catalogue.note: ff. 1–183 + 184–367 (+5 unnumbered), per the KB record

volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Volumen [III] observationum pro annis 1590-94 incl.
volumes.notes: Codex E (Opera Omnia X); Hven. Sun/Moon/planet observations for 1590–1594 (the fixed stars for these years are in Codex D / GKS 312). Four leaves of the 1593 observations are appended at its end (the rest of 1593 is in Codex K / GKS 1828).

volumes.label: Planetary observations 1595
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Quite a few observations are written in Tycho's own hand.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 182 numbered leaves + 9 unnumbered smaller leaves inserted
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes planetarum super annum 1595.
volumes.notes: Codex F (Opera Omnia X); Hven 1595. Complete; no observation missing.

volumes.label: Observations 1596–97 (Wandsbek); Kepler's declaration
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Not many entries in this codex are in Tycho's own hand. (Kepler's attestation of receipt is glued to the cover; ff. 150–157 and 161 are in David Fabricius's hand; ff. 164–186 a catalogue of 723 fixed stars.)
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 186 leaves + a fascicle of 23 leaves of miscellaneous calculations
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei planetarum et fixarum Anni Christiani 1596, Wandesburgi a 20. Octob. 1597. Adjectæ sunt in fine Observationes Davidis Fabricii, necnon Catalogus stellarum Zodiacalium et plurium fixarum ad annum 1588 completus.

facsimile.basis: Royal Danish Library, Digital Collections, object 856355; resolves (the KB catalogue record carries no link to it)

volumes.notes: Codex G (Opera Omnia X); Hven and Wandsbek. 1597 begins on fol. 93; Tycho appended David Fabricius's autograph observations. Kepler's declaration to Tycho's heirs pasted inside the front cover. Digitised: KB Digital Collections object856355.

volumes.label: Wittenberg & Benátky observations 1598–1600
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: In this codex, which lacks nothing, not many entries are in Tycho's hand. (The title on the folded board is in Tycho's hand; ff. 49–50 in Fabricius's.)
volumes.leaves_dreyer: two bundles, 108 (109 with the folded board) + 72 leaves
volumes.catalogue_title: Observationes astronomicæ factæ Wittenbergæ a Solstitio hyberno præcedente annum 1599 et variæ aliæ in arce Benatica factæ.
volumes.notes: Codex H (Opera Omnia X); Wandsbek, Wittenberg, Benátky. Two fascicles: the 2nd holds 1598 (ending with the 6 Aug 1598 Wandsbek lunar eclipse); the 1st holds 1599 (Wittenberg, then Prague) running on to 2 Feb 1600.

volumes.label: Observations 1600–1601 (Benátky & Prague)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Very few entries in it are in Tycho's hand. (The report of Tycho's final illness and death, f. 151r, is in Kepler's hand; ff. 162–165 Fabricius, f. 166 Johannes Krabbe, ff. 167–173 Kepler.)
volumes.catalogue_title: Observationes Astronomicæ annorum 1600 et 1601 in arce Cæsarea Regni Bohemici Benatica et Pragæ habitæ per instrumenta Tychonis Brahei. Accedunt Observationes, quas Tychoni misit Keplerus e Stiria initio Augusti anno 1600.
volumes.notes: Codex I (Opera Omnia X); Benátky and Prague. Ends fol. 151v with 11 Oct 1601; Kepler's hand records Tycho's final illness and death. Lacks the solar observation of 9 May 1601 and the computed Mercury position of 29 Apr 1601. Includes observations Kepler sent Tycho in 1600.

volumes.label: Seven comets 1577–1596 (mostly Tycho's hand; leaf 56 also Wittich's)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: The observations of the comet of 1577 (ff. 2–37) are all in Tycho's own hand; the 1580 comet (ff. 38–79) mostly Tycho, ff. 56–58 and a few other observations by Paul Wittich; 1582 tidy transcripts; 1585 partly original, partly copies; 1590 copied from Codex O; 1596 transcribed from Codex O.
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes septem Cometarum ab anno 1577 ad 1596 Uraniburgi, etiam magna ex parte Autogr.
volumes.notes: Hven; seven comets 1577–1596, mostly in Tycho's hand. Leaf 56 is a directly comparable Tycho-vs-Wittich pair: Tycho's autograph 1577 comet observation alongside Paul Wittich's Oct 1580 comet observations A–E, the latter authenticated by Jakob Monau's signed attestation of 23 Oct 1600 (Rosen 1981 reproduces both hands, Ryc.1–2). This leaf is documented specimen by specimen in the Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe, under the Paul Wittich discriminator.

volumes.label: Comets of 1590 & 1596
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: None of these are in Tycho's own hand, though neatly written with full astronomical descriptions; a few annotations by Tycho on the 1590 comet.
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes Cometæ anni 1590 a 23. Febr. ad 6. Martii, ut et Cometæ mense Julio 1596 apparentis.
volumes.notes: Codex O (Opera Omnia X); Hven; comets of 1590 and 1596. The cometary originals from which the fair-copies of those observations were taken.

volumes.label: Theory of Sun; lunar/planetary obs 1585–1593
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Calculations of the positions of the Moon and planets, beginning with the construction of the solar theory from an observation of 14 January 1585 (Dreyer gives no hand statement; the KB catalogue: a hand other than Longomontanus's).
volumes.catalogue_title: Fasciculus continens Theoriam Solis per observationes Lunæ ad illum et Fixas, cum observationibus Planetarum ab Ao 1585 ad 1593.
volumes.notes: Hven; theory and observations 1585–1593, in a hand other than Longomontanus's.

volumes.label: Brass-quadrant observations 1589
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Elias Olai Morsing's own book of brass-quadrant observations of 1589, made at several places in Denmark to find their polar elevations; not in Dreyer's codex list.
volumes.catalogue_title: Observationes quædam astronomicæ habitæ 1589 per Quadrantem orichalcicum Tychonis Brahe, divisionum satis capacem, in diversis locis Daniæ ad eruendas eorum Poli elevationes.
volumes.notes: Hven; brass-quadrant observations 1589, by Elias Olai (Morsing).

volumes.label: Earliest observations 1563–1582
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Not a single word in Tycho's own hand is found in the entire book.
volumes.copied_note: 1563–1577 copied from the lost octavo; December 1577 – 1581 copied from Codex B, never checked against it.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 468 pages, numbered in a later hand (70½ quires)
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes, Lipsiæ ab anno 1563-1565, Rostochii 1568, Aug. Vind. 1569-1573, Herisvadi, Hafniæ et in insula Hvenæ 1574-1582, præmissis Excerptis ex observationibus G. Frisii et Regiomontani.

volumes.notes: Codex A (Opera Omnia X); Leipzig, Rostock, Copenhagen, Hven; the 1563 Jupiter–Saturn conjunction note. Digitised: KB Digital Collections object77724.

volumes.label: Seven comets 1577–1596 (other hand)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Appears to be written by the same scribe as Codex A (the KB catalogue's 'forte Longomontani' is the catalogue's guess, not Dreyer's).
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 143 leaves + a glued-in sheet of Hagecius's remarks on the 1580 comet
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Observationes septem Cometarum ab anno 1577 ad a. 1596. Alia (forte Christ. Longomontani) manu.

scribe_attribution.basis: A hand other than the autograph comet volume GKS 1826; Dreyer notes it is possibly Longomontanus's, but this is not confirmed paleographically.

volumes.notes: A hand other than the autograph comet volume (GKS 1826); in the KB catalogue's guess 'forte Longomontani'; Dreyer (TBOO X p. XXIV) says the same scribe as Codex A.

volumes.label: Transcript of the 1585 observations (Dreyer's Codex L), with 1598–1600 calculations
volumes.dreyer_codex_note: Dreyer names A. Coll. Reg. 1829 as Codex L outright; the identification is kept as probable pending a leaf count or an image check.
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Written by the same scribe as Codex K; ff. 190–191 (two large-format leaves, a treatise on Aristotle's view of comets and one on Maestlin's hypothesis) are in Tycho's hand.
volumes.copied_note: the 1585 observations copied from Codex V (wherever Codex C diverges from V, this codex follows V); Dreyer followed it for 1585 while V was still in Vienna.
volumes.catalogue_title: Tychonis Brahei Fasciculus Observationum Solis et Planetarum, subjuncto calculo Planetarum ex observationibus annorum 1599 et 1600.

scribe_attribution.basis: Same hand as GKS 1827; possibly Longomontanus, unconfirmed. (The volume's identity is itself disputed.)

volumes.notes: Dreyer's Codex L — the 214-leaf transcript of the 1585 observations, copied from the Vienna fair-copy — is probably this volume under an imprecise modern title, but the identification is not asserted pending a leaf-count or image check, and the volume's identity remains an open question in the register. The live KB catalogue title (soeg.kb.dk; Ilsøe, Støbeskeen 1999, p. 582) reads 'Tychonis Brahei Fasciculus Observationum Solis et Planetarum, subjuncto calculo Planetarum ex observationibus annorum 1599 et 1600', in the same hand (possibly Longomontanus) as GKS 1827, whereas Dreyer, Opera Omnia X, identifies A. Coll. Reg. 1829 as his 'Codex L'. The two descriptions are irreconcilable as one volume; neighbours GKS 1827/1828/1830 align Dreyer↔KB with no offset, so a post-Dreyer rebinding/renumbering is the likely cause. The volume is recorded here per the live KB catalogue. No other candidate is found in the Royal Library's catalogue, and the catalogue title dates only the appended calculation, not the main observations.

volumes.label: Transcripts of 1593, 1590 and 1598–1600
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: All in the same hand except folios 464–478 — the scribe of Codex L.
volumes.copied_note: fasc. I (1593) the only substantial transcript of the year whose Vienna fair copy was lost; fasc. II (1590) the same observations as Codex E arranged in Codex V's order, with computed positions Codex E lacks.
volumes.leaves_dreyer: 478 leaves, all in the same hand except ff. 464–478; three fascicles (ff. 1–66 the year 1593; 67–260 the year 1590; 261–478 the years 1598–1600)
volumes.catalogue_title: Fasciculus Observationum Tychonis Brahei, alia manu [quam forte Longomontani], variorum annorum, ex quibus 1590, 1599 et 1600 expressi sunt. Addita sunt Excerpta ex quodam libro Msc. ex collegio Pragensi a M. Bacchatio Tychoni Braheo communicata.

scribe_attribution.basis: Transcripts spanning 1590–1600 — the period of Longomontanus's service, so he is the leading candidate for the engrossing hand, but this is a date-availability inference, not a confirmed identification.

volumes.notes: Codex K (Opera Omnia X). Three fascicles: the first fascicle the 1593 observations (the only substantial transcript of 1593 — the year whose Vienna fair-copy volume was lost, and which the Historia Coelestis therefore almost wholly omits); the second 1590; the third 1598, 1599 and January 1600. The single most important KB volume for recovering what the fair-copying dropped.

volumes.label: Collectio observationum (Bartholin)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: Erasmus Bartholin's copy, prepared in the 1660s to fill the lacunae of the Historia Coelestis; cited by Dreyer before December 1577 simply as 'Bartholinus'. A secure Bartholin autograph.
volumes.catalogue_title: Collectio observationum Tychonis Brahei ab Anno 1563 per Erasm. Bartholinum, præmissa ejusdem narratione de observationibus Tychonianis.
volumes.notes: Post-Tycho compilation by Erasmus Bartholin; not in the Dreyer Codex series; not digitised (reading-room only). Title: 'Collectio observationum Tychonis Brahei ab Anno 1563 … per Erasm. Bartholinum'. Observations omitted from the Historia Coelestis, including the comet observations. A secure Bartholin autograph.

volumes.label: Fair-copy observations 1582 (apographum)
volumes.dreyer_hand_statement: In the earlier volumes quite a few entries are in Tycho's own hand, whereas in the later volumes only a few are so.

transmission.event: Tycho to Landgrave Wilhelm IV: he is comparing his observations with others' and means at last to bring them into public use (TBOO VI p. 74).

In the Mechanica Tycho calls the observations 'a most rare and precious treasure' and describes their two tiers: entered in large volumes, then copied year by year into separate books arranged by subject (fol. F 2v; TBOO V pp. 109–110).
Kepler, newly arrived at Benátky, notes that Tycho will not allow him to copy the observations — 'and rightly so, for this is his treasure, in which he has spent his whole life and fortune'.
Tycho dies in Prague; the report of his illness and death is entered in Codex I (GKS 318, f. 151r) in Kepler's hand. All the observation books pass into Kepler's keeping.
By agreement with Frans Tengnagel, Tycho's son-in-law, Kepler receives 'beautifully and neatly copied' volumes of all the observations, with some autograph material among them (Friis 1875, p. 150).

Kepler's declaration to Tycho's heirs, pasted to the cover of Codex G (GKS 316): each volume is to be marked as part of his treasure, to be locked away should he die suddenly; made after his move to Linz.
Willebrord Snellius excerpts the observations of 1600–1601 in the Observationes Hassiacae (Leiden); Kepler later supposes he had access to 'the seventh tome in folio of the Protocols'.
Emperor Ferdinand II asks Duke Johann Friedrich of Württemberg to return the codices; only the fair copies are requested, and the archetypes were never returned by Kepler.
Kepler, in the Hyperaspistes, still hopes to print 'the books of observations, truly a most precious treasure of antiquity in our art'.
Kepler to Georg Brahe: he hopes soon to prepare the observations for the press.
Kepler dies at Regensburg; the edition never begun. The archetypes pass to his son Ludwig, a physician at Königsberg.

After Jakob Bartsch's death at Lauban, Albert Curtz reports to the Austrian chancellor that observations and papers are held sealed at Lauban and Dresden; a search for Kepler's manuscripts is under way.
Ludwig Kepler writes to Galileo that Christoph Scheiner has urged the Emperor to keep Tycho's observations in the Imperial Library; Ludwig moves the books to a safer place.

Albert Curtz (Albertus Curtius, S.J.) obtains the nineteen Vienna fair copies — whether from Kepler in 1621 or from Susanna Bartsch after 1634 is not known; he believes them to be the originals and finds 1593 missing.
Ludwig Kepler sells the original books to Frederik III of Denmark ('anno enim 1655, si non antea'); they are placed in the Royal Library.
Curtz prints the observations of 1582 as the Sylloge Ferdinandea (Vienna) under the anagram 'Lucius Barrettus'.
Erasmus Bartholin is commissioned to edit the observations; his receipt lists the volumes he received, the octavo of 1563–1574 among them.

The Historia Coelestis (Augsburg), Curtz's edition from the Vienna fair copies: 124 + 977 pages, without the years before 1582 and without 1593 — 'so incomplete and so carelessly compiled that it is almost useless'.
Bartholin publishes the Specimen recognitionis, a collation of the 1582 observations against the archetypes exposing the errors of the Augsburg edition.

Jean Picard, in Copenhagen to fix the latitude of Uraniborg, receives Bartholin's fair copy of the observations for printing in Paris and gives a receipt for it; Ole Rømer accompanies the archetypes to Paris.
The Paris printing reaches the year 1582 (23 quires in quarto) and stops.
Friderich Rostgaard finds the volumes in La Hire's room at the Paris Observatory — 'seven volumes in folio, seven volumes or bundles in quarto, and one volume in octavo'.
The archetypes are reclaimed by the Danish envoy and returned to the Royal Library, Copenhagen; Bartholin's copy stays in Paris, later transcribed in full by Delisle.
Lalande and Jeaurat publish the 1593 observations of Mars, Jupiter and Saturn from Bartholin's copy.
The octavo of 1563–1574 is lent from the Royal Library to Christian Hvass and never returned.
The octavo is reported in the hands of a Dane living in France (Passy); Codex A and Bartholin's GKS 310 remain its two copies.
H. C. Schumacher publishes Tycho's observations of the comet of 1585 from Codex N, and later those of 1596.
F. R. Friis publishes the observations of the seven comets.
Printing of the observations for the Opera Omnia begins (October 1913) and stops in the summer of 1916 at the end of 1583.
After the war the nineteen Vienna fair copies are lent to Copenhagen and the printing resumes.
Dreyer's edition of the observations, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia vols X–XIII, is published; the codices are described in the Prolegomena to vol. X.

desiderata.title: Eighteen stars of the 1602 print never read from the copy of the print
desiderata.text: The 2026 reading of the printed catalogue from a copy of the Progymnasmata in a private collection recovered 759 of the 777 stars; the 18 it did not read — Ursa Minor entire, Polaris included, two each in Corona Borealis, Cygnus, Ophiuchus and Hydra, one each in Aquarius, Eridanus and Triangulum — all stand on pages the passes read, at page boundaries and gutters. The catalogue is now founded on Verbunt & van Gent's keyed text and the reading is a collation witness; a second reading of these 18 rows would complete the witness.

desiderata.title: The three Vienna paper bundles (Cod. 10686, 10688, 10689)
desiderata.text: Dreyer used three large bundles of letters and papers at Vienna that carry copies of some observations (TBOO XIII p. 98 note: 'Apographum harum observationum in cod. Vindob. lat. 10689 f 26r sqq'). They are not registered here; a leaf-level description would settle which observations they witness.

desiderata.title: The archive's own star catalogues as tabled records
desiderata.text: GKS 316 ff. 164–186 (723 stars) and Cod. 10709 (296 stars near the zodiac, 1589) were printed by Dreyer at the end of TBOO XI (pp. 383–412) and in TBOO III p. 409; the appendices of TBOO XII (pp. 231–265, a catalogue to 1588) and XIII (pp. 61–77, to 1595) print further working catalogues whose manuscript witnesses the Prolegomena do not name. None is tabled star by star here.

desiderata.title: GKS 1829 as Dreyer's Codex L
desiderata.text: Dreyer names 'A. Coll. Reg. 1829' as his Codex L, the 214-leaf transcript of the 1585 observations, and himself explains its tail of 1598–1600 computations; the KB catalogue titles the volume by that tail. The identification is kept as probable pending a leaf count or an image check.

desiderata.title: Dreyer's per-passage hand notes
desiderata.text: Dreyer transcribed the marginal notes of Codex A ('in Tycho's hand but written later', 'in Longomontanus's hand again') into the edition and sets Tycho's autograph passages in italic throughout TBOO X–XIII. Harvesting those loci from the footnotes of the four volumes would give the assistants' hands a palaeographic layer the documentary-prior attributions of §8 lack.

desiderata.title: A concordance to the Historia Coelestis (1666)
desiderata.text: Curtz's edition was printed from the Vienna fair copies, without the years before 1582 and without 1593, with signs misread as numerals and pages skipped. A page-by-page concordance from the codices to the 1666 print does not exist; Bartholin's Specimen recognitionis (1668) collates the year 1582 only.

desiderata.title: The remaining pages of the printed edition
desiderata.text: The page index (§5) rests on a 2026 reading of 976 of the 1,850 pages of TBOO X–XIII, an irregular sample that omits pp. 1–18 of vol. X; the other pages are indexed only by volume and year range. archive.org holds page images and OCR of all four volumes.

desiderata.title: Facsimiles of the thirty-six volumes without one
desiderata.text: Two volumes have a public facsimile (GKS 1824, GKS 316). The Austrian National Library's catalogue records no digital copy of any of the nineteen fair copies or of Cod. 10709; the Royal Danish Library's catalogue shows no online link for the other fifteen Copenhagen volumes (probed 5 September 2026). The autograph protocols GKS 311–318 and GKS 1825–1826 are the obvious targets.

desiderata.title: Hans Crol and Johannes Eriksen in the Familia
desiderata.text: Both are candidate scribes of fair copies (Crol to his death on Hven in November 1591; Eriksen from 1596 and Tycho's secretary by 1601) and neither has a record in the Familia edition, so the attributions naming them cannot link.

desiderata.title: The Copenhagen leaf counts
desiderata.text: For the nineteen Vienna volumes the catalogue's leaf counts agree with Dreyer's to the leaf; for the Copenhagen codices Dreyer's counts and the counts an earlier version of this register carried disagreed on nine of ten, and only GKS 313 has been checked against the KB catalogue (which agrees with Dreyer). The other fourteen KB extents want the same check.

desiderata.title: The lost octavo after 1804
desiderata.text: The small octavo of 1563–1574 was in Paris in 1697, returned to Copenhagen in 1707, lent to Christian Hvass about 1778 and reported in France in 1804. Nothing later is known.

desiderata.title: Related Copenhagen manuscripts outside this register
desiderata.text: GKS 320 (the Astronomia hypothetica) and GKS 1832 (planetary tables, possibly in Bartholin's hand) are Tycho-orbit manuscripts at the Royal Library that carry no observations and are not registered here.

desiderata.title: The comet's tail in De mundi
desiderata.text: The tail measurements (16 November 1577: 17° long, 6°30′ across at its widest) and Tycho's discussion of the tail's direction are quoted from a copy of the 1588 print in a private collection; their pages in TBOO IV have not yet been located and read.

summary.title: Tycho Brahe — the precision of his star places
summary.modern_reference: Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th rev. ed. (Hoffleit & Warren 1991; VizieR V/50/catalog) — J2000 positions good to far better than an arc-second
summary.method: Tycho's ecliptic places (equinox & ecliptic of 1600) are rotated to J2000 equatorial via the full IAU-1976 precession matrix and the 1600 obliquity, then nearest-neighbour matched to the modern bright-star sky (within 40′); the separation is his positional error. Residual scatter is the error after removing the catalogue's median zero-point offset (Δλ·cosβ = +1.21′, Δβ = +0.75′). Caveat: some scatter is OCR-extraction noise in our reading of his minutes, not Tycho's own.
summary.context: For comparison: Ptolemy's Almagest places scatter by about 25′ and Ulugh Beg's (1437) by about 20′ — both of the order of 20–30′ (Verbunt & van Gent 2012); the telescope (after 1610) was needed to do materially better. nova.parallax_finding: Tycho measured the new star's distances from the principal stars of Cassiopeia (Schedir, the Chair, the knee, leg, etc.) repeatedly and carefully with his sextant, and found that throughout its whole visible duration it kept exactly the same place in the sky relative to them, 'instar Affixarum Stellarum' (like the fixed stars): it showed no proper motion and obeyed only the universal daily rotation. (A separate passage, p. 343, describes the new sextant as itself 'nulli Parallaxi obnoxium' — subject to no parallax; that phrase belongs to the instrument, not to the star.) In Caput VI ('De Stellae huius Situ... an in Elementari Regione, an ultra') he therefore argues that the star cannot lie in the elementary region below the Moon nor among the seven planetary revolutions, but in the highest, eighth (fixed-star) sphere, surpassing all the planets' orbits and the lower elementary world — directly contradicting the Aristotelian/Peripatetic dogma of an unchangeable, ingenerable celestial region.
nova.lightcurve: Tycho set down a month-by-month decline (Progymnasmata, p. 301). In November 1572 the star equalled Venus in size; through December it nearly rivalled Jupiter; in January 1573 it was a little less than Jupiter but still brighter than the first-magnitude stars. By February and March it was of the first magnitude, by April and May of the second, and through the summer it sank to the third — the size of the larger stars of Cassiopeia. By October it was of the fourth order, by the end of that year and into January barely above the fifth, in February 1574 of the sixth and smallest sort; and in March 1574 it grew so faint that it ceased altogether to be seen. Its colour changed as it faded. At its brightest, when it equalled Venus and Jupiter, it shone with a whitish (albicanti), clear and pleasant light; and Tycho affirms (p. 466) that it varied its colour, unlike the constancy of the other stars — which he takes as further proof that it belonged to the celestial and not the elementary world.
nova.dates: The narrative gives no explicit date of discovery; it begins simply 'In Novembri'. The observation span Tycho gives runs from November 1572, when the star equalled Venus, through to March 1574, when it faded below visibility — about sixteen months of continuous monitoring.

key_quotes.latin: Constitisse autem hanc Peregrinam Stellam toto suae durationis Tempore, in eodem prorsus Caeli loco, instar Affixarum Stellarum... Neque enim vllum proprium motum interea obtinere cognoscebatur, sed solummodo Reuolutioni vniuersali diurnae... obtemperauit.
key_quotes.gloss: That this strange star stood, through the whole time of its duration, in exactly the same place of the sky, like the fixed stars... For it was found to have no proper motion of its own, but obeyed only the universal daily revolution. (p. 303)

key_quotes.latin: In Nouembri (uti dixi) Veneris Stella quantitate visebatur. Per Decembrem Iouis Sidus ferme aemulabatur... donec vltimo Mense Martio adeo exilis reddita sit, vt conspici celerius prorsus desineret.
key_quotes.gloss: In November, as I said, it appeared the size of the star Venus. Through December it nearly rivalled the star Jupiter... until at last, in the month of March, it became so faint that it presently ceased to be seen at all. (p. 301)

key_quotes.latin: ...omnium aperissime ostendebat illam [inter Affixa]rum Stellarum supremam... sedes... delegisse, omniumq; Planetarum gyratio[nes] [&] infimarum elementarium Mundano exuperasse.
key_quotes.gloss: ...it showed most plainly of all that it had chosen its seat among the highest of the fixed stars, surpassing all the revolutions of the planets and the lowest elementary world. (p. 171, Liber V)

key_quotes.latin: ...obseruando videlicet easdem binas Stellas, siue Cassiopeæ, siue alterius Asterismi per vtrumq; Instrumentum, tam Vetus illud, quam Nouum Sextantem nulli Parallaxi obnoxium.
key_quotes.gloss: ...observing, that is, the same pairs of stars, whether of Cassiopeia or of another asterism, through each instrument — both that old one and the new sextant, which is subject to no parallax. (p. 343). The freedom from parallax here is the sextant's, not the star's: Tycho is comparing his two instruments, having found the older one's star-distances a few minutes too large; the passage does not bear on the star's own parallax.

comet.parallax_finding: Across the dated November 1577 - January 1578 sightings Tycho located the comet by solving spherical parallax-triangles built from its measured distances to fixed stars (e.g. triangles APB, ABC, CPB, with the apex P at the observer/Pole), the same diurnal-parallax method he applied to the Moon. The computed cometary distances came out many times the lunar distance, so the comet's parallax was far too small to put it in the sublunary air: it had to lie well above the Moon, moving forward through the zone of the planets (it crossed the region assigned to the orbs of Venus and Mercury). Page 65 of De mundi explicitly invokes the contrast with lunar parallax (the Moon near the horizon 'did not appear in the place where it really was, as optical reasoning shows'). Because a body sweeping freely through that region cannot pass through solid crystalline planetary spheres, the work's thesis is that those spheres are not real solids — the conclusion Tycho drew from the comet of 1577 — a reading confirmed by Thoren (The Lord of Uraniborg) and Mosley (Bearing the Heavens).
comet.tail: On 16 November Tycho measured the tail: 'Longitudo caudæ 17 Grad. Latitudo 6 Grad. 30 min. vbi erat latissima' — some 17 degrees long, and 6° 30′ across at its widest point. On the later nights the log fixes its endpoints by azimuth and altitude ('Initii caudæ' and 'Finis caudæ' on 30 November; 'Finis caudæ' and a second, doubtfully read 'Rursum caudæ' (?) on 1 December), from which the tail's direction across the sky follows. The leaves read here give only that — length, breadth and endpoints. Tycho's celebrated claim about the direction itself, that the tail pointed away not from the Sun but from Venus (a coincidence he later suspected of being an optical illusion, since a tail averted from the Sun would be the more natural thing), belongs to the argument of De mundi, not to these pages.
